props.title: Our Brand Is Crisis

sections.content: Our Brand Is Crisis (2015) sits in a fascinating lineage of films exploring political manipulation and campaign strategy. Sandra Bullock's role - originally written for George Clooney - adds layers to the cynical consultant archetype established in films like Wag the Dog (1997) and Primary Colors (1998). The film's Bolivia setting taps into a rich vein of Latin American political cinema, though through an distinctly American lens, similar to how Missing (1982) approached Chilean politics.

sections.content: The film's exploration of American political consultants exporting their tactics globally connects strongly to documentaries like The War Room (1993) and Knock Down the House (2019). Director David Gordon Green, known primarily for comedies like Pineapple Express (2008), brings an unexpectedly sharp edge to the material, though the film sometimes struggles between satire and serious drama, much like In the Loop (2009).

Sandra Bullock's "Calamity" Jane Bodine channels the real-life figure of James Carville, whose work in Bolivia inspired the 2005 documentary this film reimagines. The movie's critique of political marketing echoes darker works like Network (1976) and Sweet Smell of Success (1957), showing how media manipulation shapes public opinion. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Political Satire

movies.title: Network
movies.slug: A news anchor's mental breakdown becomes a ratings sensation

sections.content: While Our Brand Is Crisis attempts to balance comedy with serious commentary, it follows a tradition of political satires that includes Dr. Strangelove (1964) and Bob Roberts (1992). The film's examination of American political exports reflects themes found in Costa-Gavras's State of Siege (1972) and Z (1969), though with less overt criticism of U.S. intervention.
